title: Design a Satellite Link Assignment Under Frequency Constraints
prompt:
Design a service that assigns users to visible satellites and one of four radio frequencies, maximizing coverage within a fixed runtime budget. Each satellite has limited capacity, and nearby links on the same satellite cannot share a frequency. Some users may have no visible satellite.

Define the inputs and assignment output, including the geometric visibility and separation assumptions you need. Explain your strategy, how you verify feasibility, and how you handle changing demand and limited computation time.

response.placeholder: Define the visibility and interference predicates before selecting an assignment algorithm.
response.reference_answer:
## Normalize constraints

Precompute a bipartite visibility graph using the stated Earth and elevation geometry; edge generation is separate from assignment. For each satellite, build a conflict graph over candidate users whose beam directions violate the angular separation rule. Validate capacity, frequency count, and numeric tolerances before optimization.

## Assignment strategy

For small instances, a mixed-integer or constraint-programming formulation maximizes covered users subject to one satellite per user, capacity, and per-satellite graph coloring constraints. For large or time-bounded instances, use a deterministic heuristic: prioritize scarce users, choose a satellite by residual capacity and conflict degree, then assign the lowest feasible frequency. Local swaps or augmenting moves can recover coverage after the initial pass.

## Correctness and operations

A validator independently checks visibility, one assignment per user, capacity, and frequency conflicts before returning a plan. The response includes uncovered users with a reason such as no visibility, capacity exhaustion, or frequency conflict. Cache geometry by position version, recompute only affected neighborhoods on movement, and use stable tie-breakers for reproducible plans. Track coverage, constraint rejection reasons, solve time, approximation quality on sampled optimal baselines, and topology churn.
